author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #1: Visibility of system status
statement: Keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback within a reasonable time, so they can understand the current state and decide what to do next.
audit_check: Does the interface always show where the user is, what is happening (loading, saving, processing), and the result of each action within ~1 s?

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #2: Match between system and the real world
statement: Use words, phrases and concepts familiar to the user rather than internal jargon, and follow real-world conventions so information appears in a natural, logical order.
audit_check: Is the language the users’ language (no internal jargon, codes or system terms)? Does information follow a natural order?

title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #3: User control and freedom
statement: Users often act by mistake and need a clearly marked way out (cancel, back, undo, redo) without going through an extended process.

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #4: Consistency and standards
statement: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing; follow internal consistency and external platform and industry conventions.
audit_check: Are terms, icons, layouts and behaviors consistent within the product and with platform conventions?

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #5: Error prevention
statement: Better than good error messages is a design that prevents problems in the first place: remove error-prone conditions (slips) or check for them and ask for confirmation before committing (mistakes).
audit_check: Does the design prevent common errors (constraints, good defaults, confirmations for destructive actions, forgiving formats)?

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #6: Recognition rather than recall
statement: Minimize memory load by making elements, actions and options visible; users should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another; help should be visible or easily retrievable.
audit_check: Are options, prior answers and needed information visible when needed rather than requiring users to remember them?

author: Jakob Nielsen
title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #7: Flexibility and efficiency of use
statement: Shortcuts and accelerators, hidden from novices, can speed up interaction for experts; allow users to tailor frequent actions.

title: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics #8: Aesthetic and minimalist design
statement: Interfaces should not contain irrelevant or rarely needed information; every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and reduces their visibility.

subcategory: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
title: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design #1: Strive for consistency
statement: Use consistent sequences of actions in similar situations, identical terminology in prompts, menus and help, and consistent color, layout, capitalization and fonts; exceptions should be comprehensible and few.

subcategory: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
title: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design #2: Seek universal usability
statement: Recognize the needs of diverse users (novice to expert, age, disability, international, technology diversity); add explanations for novices and shortcuts for experts.
audit_check: Does the design serve novices and experts, and users with disabilities and different devices?

subcategory: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
title: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design #3: Offer informative feedback
statement: For every user action there should be feedback; modest for frequent and minor actions, substantial for infrequent and major ones. Visual presentation of objects of interest makes changes explicit.
audit_check: Is feedback proportional to the importance of each action?

subcategory: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design
title: Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules of Interface Design #4: Design dialogs to yield closure
statement: Organize sequences of actions into groups with a beginning, middle and end; informative feedback at completion gives satisfaction and signals readiness for the next action.
audit_check: Do multi-step tasks clearly signal completion (confirmation page/message)?
citation: Shneiderman, B. (1986). Designing the User Interface. Addison-Wesley; Shneiderman, B., Plaisant, C., Cohen, M., Jacobs, S., Elmqvist, N., & Diakopoulos, N. (2016). Designing the User Interface, 6th ed. Pearson.
